headline: Melatonin and the heart:
one study.
dek: A large health-records study tied long-term melatonin use to heart failure. Here is what it can and cannot show.
photoAlt: An older man in a cardigan holds a sleep study report.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Nov 2, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: Who was studied
glance.line: 130,828 adults with insomnia, in health records, followed for 5 years.

glance.label: What kind of study
glance.line: Observational: an association, not proof of cause. A meeting abstract, not peer reviewed.

glance.label: Status, Nov 2026
glance.line: No full paper found in PubMed. One regulator, in Saudi Arabia, has issued a safety signal.

body: In November 2025, a team at SUNY Downstate in Brooklyn presented a study at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions in New Orleans linking long-term [[/melatonin|melatonin]] use to heart failure.[^aha]

The lead author, Ekenedilichukwu Nnadi, a chief resident in internal medicine, said melatonin supplements may not be as harmless as commonly assumed, and that confirmed results could change how doctors counsel patients about sleep aids.[^aha] A year later, the study has not been confirmed.

It was not a trial; nobody was given melatonin or a dummy pill. The researchers searched electronic health records in TriNetX, a large international network of de-identified patient data, for adults with a diagnosis of insomnia.[^aha] To count as a melatonin user, a person needed at least one melatonin prescription and at least 365 days of exposure in the record; the comparison group had no melatonin recorded at all.[^abstract] Anyone already diagnosed with heart failure, or prescribed other sleeping pills such as benzodiazepines, was left out.[^aha] The team then matched 65,414 users with 65,414 non-users on age, sex, other illnesses, heart drugs, lab results, vital signs and how much health care they used, and followed the records for five years.[^abstract] The 130,828 people averaged 55.7 years old, and 61.4% were women.[^aha]

The main finding: over five years, heart failure was newly diagnosed in 3,021 melatonin users (4.6%) and 1,797 non-users (2.7%), a hazard ratio of 1.89, or about 89% higher.[^abstract] Hospital stays coded for heart failure were recorded for 19.0% of users and 6.6% of non-users, and 7.8% of users died from any cause compared with 4.3% of non-users.[^abstract] When the team narrowed the melatonin group to people with at least two prescriptions filled 90 days or more apart, the result for heart failure was similar.[^abstract] The authors concluded that their findings “challenge the perception of melatonin as a benign chronic therapy and underscore the need for randomized trials to clarify its cardiovascular safety profile.”[^abstract]

The AHA spelled out the limits itself. The study was an abstract, and the association noted that abstracts at its meetings “are not peer-reviewed, and the findings are considered preliminary until published as full manuscripts in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.”[^aha] It was observational, and the release said plainly that it “cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship.”[^aha] People with worse insomnia, depression or anxiety may be more likely both to take melatonin and to develop heart trouble, and the researchers had no data on how severe anyone’s insomnia was or on other psychiatric conditions.[^aha]

How melatonin use was measured affects the comparison. The database mixes countries where melatonin needs a prescription, such as the United Kingdom, with countries where it does not, such as the United States, and patients’ locations were not available to the researchers.[^aha] Because only melatonin entered in a medical record counted, anyone buying it over the counter in the US would have landed in the comparison group.[^aha] The comparison group may have included people who bought it over the counter. Marie-Pierre St-Onge, a Columbia University sleep researcher who was not involved, noted that melatonin, “at least in the U.S., is not indicated for the treatment of insomnia.”[^aha]

That last point goes to how melatonin is sold in the US. It is a dietary supplement, not an approved drug, and FDA says that under the 1994 supplement law, “FDA does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed.”[^suppqa] The National Institutes of Health adds that “in several other countries, melatonin is available only with a prescription and is considered a drug.”[^nccih] In the European Union, for example, a slow-release melatonin tablet, Circadin, is authorised for short-term insomnia in people 55 and over, and “can only be obtained with a prescription.”[^circadin]

In 2026, other researchers responded. In March, a letter in the Journal of Pineal Research by researchers in Pisa and Wisconsin critically re-examined the heart failure study and another paper questioning melatonin’s safety.[^pineal] In May, two Vanderbilt cardiologists published an analysis in Open Heart using the US national health survey known as NHANES, from 1999 to 2018. Melatonin users there differed sharply from non-users, especially in sleep problems and depression, and “recent melatonin use was not significantly associated with prevalent composite cardiovascular disease or heart failure.”[^openheart] They called it a counterpoint, not proof of safety.[^openheart] In June, Greek researchers proposed a possible mechanism involving the hormone prolactin, while stressing that the signal came from “a single, as-yet unpublished conference abstract that has not undergone peer review or independent validation.”[^wjem]

One regulator has acted. On April 19, 2026, the Saudi Food and Drug Authority published a safety signal asking health professionals to be aware of heart failure with melatonin.[^sfda] Its search of the World Health Organization’s global database found four case reports, which it said “lacked sufficient information for a proper assessment”;[^sfda] it cited the AHA abstract and concluded the evidence was “suggestive for causal association between Melatonin and Cardiac failure.”[^sfda] The agency describes a signal as uncertain and preliminary by nature.[^sfda] No US action on melatonin and the heart was found for this story.

Why it matters to men: the study’s average participant was in their mid-fifties, and in the US melatonin can be bought and taken nightly for years without a prescription. NIH says “information on the long-term safety of supplementing with melatonin is lacking.”[^nccih] The heart-failure finding comes from one records study, not yet peer reviewed.

The central question is still open: does melatonin itself affect the heart, or do long-term users simply differ from non-users? As of November 2, 2026, a PubMed search found no full paper from Nnadi’s team.[^pubmed] The study’s own authors say the answer needs randomized trials.[^abstract] Until a full manuscript appears, or a trial reports, the finding has not been confirmed.
